content: The term WASH in health care facilities refers to the provision of water, sanitation, hygiene, health care waste management, and environmental cleaning infrastructure and services throughout all areas of a health care facility. These facilities may be located in either urban or rural settings. WASH services are essential for delivering quality health care. Without these services, critical health goals, such as reducing maternal and neonatal mortality, curbing the spread of antimicrobial resistance, and preventing and containing disease outbreaks, cannot be achieved. Furthermore, WASH services are integral to the dignity and experience of care for both patients and staff. Functional and accessible toilets with menstrual hygiene facilities, as well as safe drinking water, uphold basic human rights and ensure respect for individuals. The renewed emphasis on primary health care services, as highlighted in the Astana Declaration, and the focus on reducing early childhood deaths through initiatives like the Every Child Alive Campaign, present an unprecedented opportunity to address WASH as part of health system strengthening. The 2019 WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) SDG baseline report provides global, regional, and national estimates for WASH in health care facilities. The data reveal significant inadequacies in all types of WASH services in these facilities. For instance, 2 billion people lack basic water services, and 1.5 billion lack basic sanitation services in health care settings. Many more are served by facilities without hand hygiene materials or proper waste segregation. WASH services are more commonly available in hospitals and urban areas compared to non-hospital and rural health care facilities. Non-hospital facilities are twice as likely to lack water or sanitation services compared to hospitals, and similar disparities exist between urban and rural areas. The largest data gaps pertain to hand hygiene, health care waste management, and cleaning practices. WHO and UNICEF have compiled data from 125 countries, covering over 560,000 health care facilities. Efforts are underway to integrate global WASH indicators into national monitoring systems and external surveys. Advocacy for this inclusion is critical to improving data availability, enabling informed actions, and ensuring accountability. The JMP updates global figures every two years, with the next report planned for 2021. Since the launch of the global action plan on WASH in health care facilities in 2015, significant progress has been made. WASH standards are now included in many global health standards and tools, which are actively implemented in over 40 countries with government leadership and support from 35 partners. In 2018, the WHO/UNICEF JMP developed a harmonized set of global WASH indicators for health care facilities, which are used to report progress on SDG 6. These indicators have been integrated into national health information systems, health facility assessment surveys, and specific programs focusing on maternal and child health, vaccines, cholera, sepsis, and neglected tropical diseases. The WHO/UNICEF Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT), which employs a quality improvement approach to prioritize and address WASH risks, has been implemented in over 20 countries. In March 2018, the UN Secretary-General issued a global call to action on WASH in health care facilities, urging committed leadership and greater accountability for providing WASH services in all health care settings. In response, WHO and UNICEF have established global targets for achieving universal access to WASH in health care facilities. By 2022, 60% of all health care facilities globally and in each SDG region should have at least basic WASH services, increasing to 80% by 2025 and 100% by 2030. For countries that have already achieved universal basic WASH services, higher service levels are being defined and monitored, with the goal of achieving these higher levels universally in 80% of such countries by 2030. To make progress, countries can take eight practical steps: conduct a situational analysis and assessment; set targets and define a national roadmap; establish national standards and accountability mechanisms; improve and maintain infrastructure; monitor progress and review data; develop the health workforce; engage communities; and conduct operational research and share learning. These steps are detailed in the Practical steps to achieve universal access document, which includes country examples. Implementation will vary based on country priorities and contexts, and additional steps may be pursued as needed. Member States, UN agencies, and partners are encouraged to commit to action. Over 35 partners, along with UN agencies, have already made concrete commitments to improve WASH in health care facilities. The next step is to secure universal, action-oriented commitments on water, sanitation, and hygiene at international, regional, national, and local levels. Mechanisms to support and track progress include the WHO/UNICEF JMP, which compiles data on coverage, and the UN-Water Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking-Water, which collects data on policies and targets. In January 2019, a draft World Health Assembly resolution on WASH in health care facilities was sponsored by 10 Member States and unanimously approved by the WHO Executive Board. This resolution calls for Member States to engage in the eight practical steps, starting with national assessments, roadmaps, and new targets and standards for WASH in health care facilities. Member States will report progress to WHO every two years. Countries across all regions are taking action on some or all of the eight practical steps. Examples include Cambodia conducting a health systems situational analysis, Ghana developing a national costed WASH strategy for health care facilities, Serbia and Lebanon developing national standards, Tanzania strengthening the cleaning workforce, Liberia providing mentoring and supervision to improve services, and Indonesia, the Philippines, Nepal, and Vietnam adopting green health care waste management approaches. These efforts demonstrate that significant progress can be achieved even in resource-limited settings. The public can support the UN Secretary-General’s Call to Action by understanding the WASH situation in their country. If data are unavailable, communities and health care facility users should demand that health authorities and facility managers track and share data and progress on improving WASH services. Care seekers should recognize that access to safe water and sanitation services is a fundamental right. They should participate in the design and improvement of WASH services and advocate for clean, safe health care facilities with accessible toilets and safe drinking water. Additionally, health care providers should be held accountable for practicing good hand hygiene and serving as role models for the community. For more information, the WHO/UNICEF WASH in health care facilities website provides tools, technical guidance, country case studies, news, and events related to the topic. You can also sign up for regular updates through the WHO/UNICEF WASH newsletter.
